transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-10
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Amit (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Lina (NexaHealth Head AI), Rajiv (Platform), Sophie (CTO), Tom (Data Eng)

Auto-generated sections (may be imperfect):
Summary:
Quick discovery with NexaHealth evaluating Redwood for embeddings + rerank POC. Main concerns: vector DB choice and indexing strategy, upsert throughput and bulk import, hybrid search (vector + keyword), latency targets for reranking, security (VPC/KMS) and Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: send benchmark spreadsheet and schedule POC kickoff.

Topics covered:
- current embedding dimensions (512 vs 1536) and model consistency
- candidate generation vs cross-encoder rerank architecture
- vector store throughput (qps, upsert, bulk load)
- HNSW tuning, shard/replica strategy, and cold-start behavior
- tradeoffs between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC)
- SOC2/KMS/peering requirements

Action items (also in metadata): see above list

Transcript body (timestamps approx, some transcription noise):
[00:00] Maya: okay so hi everyone, thank you for joining. quick intros — i'm maya from Redwood, amit and jordan are with me, wanna start with who you are on the call?
[00:08] Lina: yep hi i'm lina, head of ai at nexahealth. Tom and rajiv are here to talk infra and the dataset. sophie popped in to listen.
[00:15] Rajiv: hi all.
[00:17] Amit: great thanks Lina. goal today is to understand your vector workload — dims, qps, latency SLOs, current vector store, and decide a POC plan.
[00:26] Tom: we currently have about 1.2 million clinical note embeddings, using a 1536-d encoder. we also have logs from search flow — about 150 qps peak, maybe 300 qps for short bursts.
[00:35] Jordan: got it, and where are you storing them today? pinecone?
[00:38] Tom: we tried pinecone for a pilot last year, but ended up using an in-house FAISS service on k8s. maintenance is heavy, and we're seeing recall drop when scale changes.
[00:46] Sophie: and we need HIPAA-friendly options too, so a private deployment or VPC peering matters.
[00:52] Maya: understood. two big axes here: candidate generation latency (ANN search) and rerank latency (cross-encoder). do you aim to run reranker synchronously?
[01:01] Lina: yes, at least for the top-10 candidate set we want sub-300ms for the full rerank in critical flows. non-critical can be async.
[01:08] Amit: that is tight for a cross-encoder, but doable if you limit candidates and use batching. e.g., 10 candidates with a reasonably small cross-encoder model on a Dedicated pool can hit ~200-250ms.
[01:19] Rajiv: what does that look like for throughput? if we have 150 qps sustained and 300 bursts, that sounds like a lot.
[01:25] Amit: right — you'll need both good ANN latency and a rerank pool that can autoscale. typical pattern: use an ANN for candidate gen (HNSW, PQ with FAISS or Qdrant) at <20ms, then rerank on GPU instances with batching and the runtime's KV cache to avoid cold-token overhead. for 150 qps with 10 candidates each that's 1500 cross-encoder calls per second if done naively; batching shrinks that.
[01:45] Tom: 1500 calls/sec sounds crazy — can you give an example config?
[01:49] Amit: Sure — e.g., if you run a cross-encoder that processes batches of 32 pairs and achieves 2500 pairs/sec per GPU, you'd need like 1-2 GPUs for baseline, autoscaling to 4-5 for bursts. but it depends on model size and batching efficiency. also, Redwood Optimize suggests model distillation + quantization to reduce cost.
[02:08] Lina: on the vector store side, what about upsert throughput? we have nightly bulk imports and also streaming updates.
[02:15] Jordan: two paths — bulk import and streaming upserts. bulk import handled via batch load (multi-threaded, parallel shards) — we can do 500k-1M imports in a maintenance window with Dedicated. streaming upserts at production QPS need write throughput planning — many vector DBs have slower upserts. which db are you leaning toward?
[02:29] Tom: we'd prefer an open-source stack — currently FAISS but open to Milvus or Qdrant, maybe keep Pinecone as fallback.
[02:36] Amit: all workable. note per-upsert latency and replica sync differ. Milvus and Qdrant have good bulk import patterns, Milvus needs tuning around segment flush and compaction; Qdrant is nicer for near-realtime with ram-backed shards. FAISS often prefers periodic rebuilds which can be disruptive.
[02:51] Rajiv: any guidance on dimensionality? we use 1536 dims — is there pressure to reduce to 768?
[02:57] Jordan: 1536 is common for models like text-embed-ada-ish; down-projection reduces memory and improves ANN speed but may hurt recall. Redwood's Optimize can run evaluation to compare 1536 vs PCA/OPQ to 768 to see recall drop off. many customers keep 1536 for medical text where nuance matters.
[03:15] Sophie: from a cost perspective, if we halve dims we halve index size roughly so cheaper storage and potentially faster searches — is the platform supporting mixed-dimension indices?
[03:24] Maya: Redwood supports storing embeddings and routing to different index types. you can have a tiered strategy: keep full-dimension recent docs, lower-dim summaries for older items, and run rerank only on full-dimension hits. it's a bit of engineering but we've seen good unit-cost improvements.
[03:38] Lina: hybrid search — we also rely on important keywords in clinical notes. how do you do vector+keyword hybrid?
[03:44] Amit: two common approaches: 1) append a BM25/elastic search filter to narrow candidates before ANN; or 2) include token-level metadata or boosted term vectors in the ANN query. we usually recommend candidate filters with boolean constraints in the vector DB (e.g., Qdrant supports filter expressions), then run ANN, then rerank. this avoids diluting vector similarity with keywords.
[04:03] Tom: what about recall tuning for HNSW? efSearch / efConstruction tradeoffs?
[04:08] Jordan: efConstruction affects build cost and initial recall; efSearch affects query latency/recall. setting efSearch to 128-200 increases recall but increases query time. we typically start with efConstruction=200, efSearch=128 and tune from logs. Redwood console can surface recall vs latency curves to pick a sweet spot.
[04:26] Rajiv: cold starts — when you spin up replicas how long to warm? we can't afford long warm times because traffic patterns are spiky.
[04:33] Amit: warm-up includes loading vectors into memory, HNSW graph in RAM, and kernel jit caching on inference side. Dedicated with pinned capacity avoids most of this. for Hosted we recommend pre-warm hooks (a small synthetic traffic ramp) and keep-alive to avoid full cold starts. Private on-prem is similar to Dedicated if you reserve nodes.
[04:53] Lina: security — we need VPC peering, KMS, and audit logs; can you confirm Redwood Private meets this?
[04:59] Maya: yes, Private gives customer-managed networking, KMS integrations and full audit logs. Dedicated also supports VPC peering and KMS for encryption at rest. Hosted can meet SOC2 controls but for HIPAA we usually suggest Dedicated or Private. We'll share the security pack.
[05:12] Sophie: any legal caveats with third-party vector stores? we want data residency and control.
[05:17] Maya: if you use our Private deployment, the control plane can be customer-hosted, and data stores can remain in your VPC or on-prem. for Hosted, we provide region controls and contractual commitments.
[05:26] Tom: back to performance — how do you measure end-to-end latency in Redwood Console? we want token-level cost too.
[05:31] Jordan: console shows per-request breakdown: ANN time, network, rerank model time, token generation, and cost estimates. you can slice by route/model and inspect worst latency percentiles.
[05:40] Lina: can we run a side-by-side benchmark with our dataset?
[05:43] Maya: yes, that's the POC plan. two tracks: 1) index your embeddings into a chosen vector DB behind Redwood (Dedicated or Private) and run sample queries; 2) run hosted small-scale to validate rerank quality. we'll deliver a benchmark sheet for upsert and qps.
[05:56] Rajiv: for the POC, what is the recommended dataset size? we can provide 500k sample docs or the full 1.2M.
[06:02] Amit: start with 500k for faster cycles; include the high-variance docs that stress recall. we also need the ingest pattern: bulk nightly + streaming updates ~200/sec.
[06:11] Tom: ingestion pattern is about 200 updates per sec during business hours, occasional spikes at 800.
[06:17] Jordan: okay we'll size autoscaling accordingly and provide example helm charts for Dedicated.
[06:22] Lina: any gotchas with vector versioning? if we update embedding models will Redwood handle reindexing gracefully?
[06:29] Maya: Redwood supports model version pinning and rolling reindexes — you can do blue/green indexing: create a new index, import, then flip traffic using rollout policies. Console shows the delta in recall so you don't regress.
[06:40] Sophie: is there any limit on embedding dimensions or vector types?
[06:43] Amit: generally no hard limit; practical limits bound memory. typical dims 256-2048 are common. some DBs are more optimized for float32 vs int8 quantized stores. we can advise based on your budget.
[06:54] Tom: can Redwood host the index or do we have to manage the vector DB?
[06:58] Maya: options: Hosted — Redwood manages everything (we use our managed vector store and can integrate with 3rd-party stores); Dedicated — reserved capacity where we can operate the vector layer for you; Private — you host in your VPC/on-prem and Redwood control plane orchestrates. For strict compliance, Private is typical.
[07:12] Lina: pricing question — how is reranking charged? per-token / per-inference?
[07:17] Jordan: rerank using cross-encoders is charged per inference and per-token depending on model; Redwood shows both inference units and token units. Dedicated often gives predictable committed throughput pricing. We'll include example cost projection in the spreadsheet.
[07:29] Rajiv: can we run a cheap distilled reranker for a first pass?
[07:32] Amit: yes, cascade architecture: cheap bi-encoder or interaction-lite model first, then cross-encoder on top-k. That reduces GPU cost a lot. We can show sample configurations.
[07:42] Tom: how does Redwood handle vector TTL / deletion / soft deletes? we need auditability and retention windows per policy.
[07:49] Maya: index-level policies and per-document metadata; delete operations trigger tombstones and can be scheduled for compaction. Audit logs record deletes for compliance. We'll share the retention/config docs.
[07:59] Lina: what's the expected timeline for a POC?
[08:02] Maya: if we get datasets in a week, we can spin a baseline POC in 2 weeks: import, configure ANN and rerank, run benchmarks and a short quality eval. full integration with SSO/KMS may take longer.
[08:12] Sophie: ok that sounds reasonable. let's talk about follow-ups.
[08:15] Maya: next steps recap — we'll send benchmark spreadsheet, security pack, and a POC kickoff invite. Amit will follow up with HNSW tuning notes and an upsert script.
[08:26] Rajiv: one last quick question — how do you handle multi-tenancy and isolation in Dedicated?
[08:31] Amit: Dedicated uses reserved pools per customer; network isolation and RBAC at the cluster level; plus per-tenant metrics and cost breakdowns. For stricter isolation, Private puts the data plane in your environment.
[08:43] Tom: thanks. also curious about warm-up for the cross-encoder models — do you recommend always keeping at least one GPU warm?
[08:49] Jordan: yes, for latency SLOs keep a warm baseline; autoscaling then adds capacity for bursts. We'll provide cost impact examples.
[08:57] Lina: thanks everyone, this was helpful. I will coordinate with Rajiv/Tom to get the dataset and timeline.
[09:03] Maya: great, we'll send the sheets and a proposed POC plan by EOD tomorrow. Appreciate the time.
[09:09] (call ends)
